item.title: Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models [1] (arXiv preprint, September 2025), Mark Steyvers, Catarina Belem, and Padhraic Smyth (UC Irvine) show that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on consistency-derived confidence targets raises both calibration and discrimination of verbalized LLM confidence (within domain, across new domains, and across two different metacognitive task formats), but only when the training data covers both formats jointly.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in decision-making contexts, but when they present answers without signaling low confidence, users may unknowingly act on erroneous outputs. Prior work shows that LLMs maintain internal uncertainty signals, yet their expressed confidence is often miscalibrated and poorly discriminates between correct and incorrect answers. We investigate whether supervised fine-tuning can improve models’ ability to communicate uncertainty and whether such improvements generalize across tasks and domains. We fine-tune LLMs on datasets spanning general knowledge, mathematics, and open-ended trivia, and evaluate two metacognitive tasks: (1) single-question confidence estimation, where the model assigns a numeric certainty to its answer, and (2) pairwise confidence comparison, where the model selects which of two answers it is more likely to answer correctly. We assess generalization to unseen domains, including medical and legal reasoning. Results show that fine-tuning improves calibration (alignment between stated confidence and accuracy) and discrimination (higher confidence for correct vs. incorrect responses) within and across domains. However, gains are task-specific: training on single-question calibration does not transfer to pairwise comparison, and vice versa. Multitask fine-tuning yields broader gains, lowering calibration error and strengthening discrimination in out-of-domain evaluations. This suggests that uncertainty communication in LLMs is trainable but requires multitask training to generalize effectively.

Methods

The authors define two metacognitive tasks that probe the same underlying ability — verbalizing internal uncertainty — through different output formats:

  • Single-question confidence (S) — the model emits an answer plus a numeric confidence (e.g. “my confidence is 0.75”). Scored with two metrics: Expected Calibration Error (ECE), the bin-weighted average gap between predicted confidence and empirical accuracy (11 bins of width 0.1), and Area Under the Curve (AUC), the probability that the model assigns higher confidence to a correct answer than to an incorrect one.
  • Pairwise confidence comparison (C) — given two questions, the model picks which one it is more likely to answer correctly. Scored with two AUC variants: AUC (does the selection match the question with the higher consistency-derived reference confidence?) and AUC (does the selection match which question the model actually answers correctly?).

Both formats are illustrated side-by-side in Figure 1.

Training labels are derived from the model’s own behavior, not human annotations. For each training question the authors sample the model multiple times, compute a consistency score across samples and the modal answer, then build two parallel training sets:

  • Single-question targets — each training question gets two targets: an answer target and a confidence target. The answer target is the modal answer — the answer that appears most often across the multiple samples drawn from the model. The confidence target comes from a calibration mapping that does use ground-truth correctness:
    • Across the labeled training-set questions, the authors compute consistency scores, bin questions by score, and record the empirical accuracy (fraction actually correct, using ground truth) in each bin — yielding a curve that maps consistency accuracy.
    • For each training question with consistency , the confidence target is (small noise added to prevent the model from memorizing the discrete bin boundaries) — i.e., “questions whose samples agree this much come out right this often, on average.”
  • Pairwise targets — each training example is a pair of questions and gets a single selection target: which of the two the model should claim higher confidence on. The supervision label is whichever question has the higher consistency score (the ranking is what matters here, so the raw consistency score is enough — no calibration-curve lookup needed).

The full pipeline — sample, score, look up calibrated target, build training set — is laid out in Figure 2.

They fine-tune two base models (GPT-4.1-mini via OpenAI’s SFT API and Llama-3.1-70B locally) under three training conditions — S (single-question targets only), C (pairwise targets only), or C+S (both jointly, the multitask condition) — on three within-domain corpora: MMLU-PRO (M), GSM8K (G), and TriviaQA (T), plus the M+G+T mixture. Held-out evaluation uses both within-domain test splits and three out-of-domain corpora: TruthfulQA, MetaMedQA, and LegalBench. Significance is assessed with a paired bootstrap over 1,000 resamples.

Results

Evaluation covers six datasets across two base models, two task formats (single-question S, pairwise C), three training conditions (S, C, C+S as defined above), and three generalization tiers (within-domain, across-domain, across-task). ECE measures calibration error (lower is better); AUC measures discrimination (higher is better). One thing to keep in mind for interpreting the deltas: the SFT loss never sees ground-truth answer labels directly — training tuples pair each question with the model’s own modal answer and a confidence scalar. Ground truth enters the pipeline only offline to fit the consistency-to-accuracy curve that produces those scalars. The recipe is therefore not aimed at improving factual accuracy, and Appendix Table A3 reports that accuracy is in fact similar before vs. after fine-tuning across all conditions. Pre/post deltas in ECE and AUC can therefore be read primarily as changes in confidence behavior, not in answer quality.

The cover figure (Figure 3) shows the within-domain calibration curves at a glance: baselines (cyan) sit below the diagonal, with confidence values clustered in [0.85, 0.95] but actual accuracy much lower at those points — overconfidence; the fine-tuned curves (pink) hug the diagonal across the full [0, 1] range. Table 1 quantifies the effect across all three generalization tiers.

The findings:

  • Within-domain SFT works on the trained format (Table 1 rows 1–6, Table 2 rows 1–6). On the format the model is trained on, ECE collapses and AUC lifts substantially across all three corpora. Multi-domain training (M+G+T) does not interfere with per-domain gains.
  • Cross-domain transfer holds for the trained format (rows 7–9). Single-task SFT trained on M+G+T improves both metrics on TruthfulQA, MetaMedQA, and LegalBench — except on TruthfulQA, where ECE actually rises because the baseline was already well-calibrated there.
  • Across-task transfer fails — and can backfire (rows 10–12). Pairwise-only SFT worsens single-question calibration on the already-calibrated domain and yields no AUC gain. Single-task SFT tested on the pairwise format shows the symmetric failure. Format isn’t a free transfer.
  • Multitask SFT (C+S) recovers and adds (rows 13–15). Joint training lifts AUC and drops ECE on the out-of-domain evaluations, beating single-task SFT alone — except again on TruthfulQA, where the already-calibrated-domain regression persists.
  • Llama-3.1-70B partially diverges. Single-question gains mirror GPT-4.1-mini, but multitask fine-tuning fails to lift Llama’s out-of-domain pairwise discrimination relative to comparison-only training. The “multitask helps both formats” headline is GPT-specific.

Figure 4 plots the OOD calibration curves under multitask SFT — the diagonal-hugging gain is largest on LegalBench, where the baseline was most overconfident.

My Notes

  • The “self-consistency only” framing is overstated: the paper says “the model is not trained using ground-truth correctness signals” (§2.1). True at the loss level: the SFT loss doesn’t reference per-question GT labels. But the confidence target depends on , the empirical accuracy at consistency , computed by comparing modal answers to ground truth (§4.3.2). The recipe inherits the label dependency of any supervised calibration method.

  • What this paper actually adds: consistency-based SFT is prior art (the authors cite three earlier works). The contribution is the 3×3×3 grid (training condition × generalization tier × test domain), which documents three failure modes: across-task transfer fails, well-calibrated domains regress under joint training, and Llama doesn’t inherit the multitask benefit on the comparison task. Does semantic entropy [2] or the verbal-confidence work in Kadavath et al. [3] have similar transfer failures? Their evaluations don’t run this grid.

  • S and C may be separable abilities: the paper concludes single-question (S) and pairwise (C) tasks are “distinct metacognitive routines, not interchangeable manifestations of a single uncertainty signal” (§2.3). The evidence: training only on S doesn’t improve C performance, and training only on C doesn’t improve S (Table 1 rows 10–12, Table 2 rows 10–12). Open question: is the underlying uncertainty signal also format-specific, or does the split only emerge at verbalization? AbstentionBench [4], metacognition atlas [5], and compliance-trap [6] each catalog one uncertainty failure mode (abstention, monitorability, prompt-regime collapse); this paper adds format-specific transfer. None has measured them together.

  • Calibration cost on already-calibrated domains: on TruthfulQA the baseline ECE is already 0.10; multitask SFT raises it to 0.13. A training intervention that helps most domains can hurt a well-behaved one. The Cacioli atlas [5] showed monitorability varies by 0.3+ AUC across MMLU subjects from the same base model; this paper adds that an SFT intervention’s sign can flip with domain. Evaluate the target domain’s pre-SFT calibration before deploying.

  • Compare to the test-time SVM harness: a recent metacognitive harness for Sonnet-4.6 [7] solves the same problem at the inference layer instead of via SFT. The harness leaves the model untouched and fits a small external SVM mapping , where FOK is the model’s pre-solve confidence rating and JOL is the post-solve rating. Inference flow: model emits FOK; if low, allocate more reasoning budget; model solves and emits JOL; SVM gives ; if , accept, else draw more attempts and aggregate. Both methods need GT correctness offline (this paper to fit , the harness to fit the SVM on a 100-question anchor set). Trade-off: the harness needs only ~100 labeled questions per base model and produces a tiny artifact but refits per model; this paper needs a larger labeled set and full SFT but produces a self-contained model that emits a calibrated confidence number from one sample at inference.

  • Practical alternative to abstention-from-prompting: the compliance-trap result [6] showed structural prompt constraints degrade frontier abstention by up to 30 accuracy points. This paper offers a weight-level analogue: train calibration into the model directly, so the prompt has less to override at inference. Follow-up: rerun compliance-trap on a model fine-tuned with this recipe; does the 8–30 point drop shrink?

References

  1. Steyvers, M., Belem, C., and Smyth, P. “Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2510.05126), September 30, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05126

  2. Farquhar, S., Kossen, J., Kuhn, L., and Gal, Y. “Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy.” Nature 630, pages 625–630 (arXiv:2406.15927), June 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15927

  3. Kadavath, S., Conerly, T., Askell, A., Henighan, T., Drain, D., Perez, E., Schiefer, N., Hatfield-Dodds, Z., DasSarma, N., Tran-Johnson, E., et al. “Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2207.05221), July 11, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221

  4. Kirichenko, P., Ibrahim, M., Chaudhuri, K., and Bell, S. J. “AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions.” NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (arXiv:2506.09038). https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038

  5. Cacioli, J.-P. “Domain-level metacognitive monitoring in frontier LLMs: A 33-model atlas.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.06673), April 21, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06673

  6. Kumar, R. “The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.02398), May 14, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02398

  7. Cao, Q., Wang, Y., Qin, P., Zhang, S., and Xie, P. “LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.14186), May 13, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14186

Related Posts

  • Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback: the prompt-level analogue to this paper’s weight-level fix, eliciting calibrated verbal confidence without fine-tuning.
  • LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling: solves the same calibration problem at inference with an external SVM instead of SFT, the test-time counterpart contrasted in My Notes.
  • Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know: the foundational verbalized-confidence result this paper extends, showing models hold internal uncertainty signals that SFT can sharpen.
  • Domain-Level Metacognitive Monitoring in Frontier LLMs: A 33-Model Atlas: documents that calibration varies sharply by domain, reinforcing this paper’s finding that an SFT intervention’s sign can flip with the target domain.
  • A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses: unpacks the ECE and AUC metrics this paper reports, and what each one hides.

item.title: Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In the May 6, 2026 episode of the AIU Community channel, Daron Acemoglu — MIT Institute Professor and 2024 Nobel laureate in Economic Sciences — argues that AI as currently deployed is going in the wrong direction. The technology is being pushed to replace humans rather than augment them, the productivity gains aren’t showing up, the AI bubble is real and structurally fragile, and the same democratic conversations that built shared prosperity in the post-war period have to be rebuilt now if AI’s labor-market effects aren’t going to break liberal democracy itself.

The main points, each linking to the supporting passage in the transcript:

  • Reactive vs. proactive AI philosophy. Putting guardrails on AI as it goes wrong is “always going to be defensive.” The harder, more important question is what do we want from AI, and what is it actually capable of, before deciding which directions to scale.
  • Augment, don’t replace. The vision of AI in every electrician’s, nurse’s, teacher’s hands — helping them handle complexity that’s increasing rapidly — is technically easier than building agents that try to do those jobs autonomously. We’re choosing the harder, less-useful path. The augmentation-vs-automation framing is well-trodden ground; see also Steve Miller on the same question.
  • The productivity gap is real and structural. Companies adopting AI in the wild — not in the lab — aren’t seeing huge productivity benefits. Workers end up “babysitting AI” in flux organizations, losing tasks they were good at, with rising stress and stagnant wages.
  • The tax-code asymmetry. US tax law subsidizes capital and penalizes labor: compute spending amortizes, capital gains escape, but every worker carries payroll tax + healthcare + income tax. That asymmetry quietly pushes every CEO toward automation. Taxing compute or AI profits would close part of the gap.
  • The AI bubble. The path to half-a-trillion or trillion-dollar profits to amortize current AI capex doesn’t have a monetization model — “people are not going to pay huge amounts to ask ChatGPT which restaurant to go to.” If the bubble bursts in an AI-dependent economy, the recession is a double whammy and itself becomes a threat to democratic institutions. The downside-scenario mechanics are sketched out in detail by Citrini Research’s 2028 Intelligence Crisis thought exercise.
  • Liberal democracy hangs on AI’s direction. Shared prosperity in the post-war US came through the labor market — wages and good jobs — rather than through redistribution. If AI continues replacing rather than augmenting, the labor market can’t deliver shared prosperity, and liberal democracy loses the underlying conditions that kept it functional.

I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post — the YouTube auto-caption transcript, sliced into editorial chapters and topic subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor’s-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for details.

YouTube chapters (jump to the enriched transcript below, or watch on YouTube — the video has no official chapter markers, so the timestamps and titles are editorial):

  • 0:00 — Reactive vs. proactive AI philosophy (YouTube)
  • 3:09 — AI in schools: what the early evidence shows (YouTube)
  • 7:17 — Augment workers, don’t replace them (YouTube)
  • 10:50 — Inequality and which jobs are next (YouTube)
  • 13:26 — China, zero-sum thinking, and global AI governance (YouTube)
  • 16:37 — Advice to college kids and the case for democratic conversation (YouTube)
  • 19:14 — Defining AGI and why it’s hard to reach (YouTube)
  • 21:17 — How prosperous societies were built (YouTube)
  • 26:30 — The AI bubble and its monetization gap (YouTube)
  • 29:07 — Macro fragility and the 1970s parallel (YouTube)
  • 31:14 — Liberal democracy in crisis (YouTube)
  • 34:24 — Closing: change the conversation (YouTube)

My Notes

  • Tax-code asymmetry, the strongest claim. Acemoglu’s most consequential point here is structural rather than technological. Capital purchases (compute, GPUs, equipment) amortize and benefit from interest-rate subsidies; hiring a worker triggers payroll tax, healthcare, and income tax. That asymmetry biases corporate decision-making toward automation independent of whether AI can actually do the job. Even if frontier-model progress flatlined tomorrow, the structural push to substitute capital for labor would continue, because it’s a tax arbitrage. Most labor-economics framings of AI miss this because the policy mechanism sits upstream of capability.

  • The 50%-reliability bar is too low. METR’s time-horizon benchmark reports the task length at which a frontier model maintains 50% completion rate. Useful as a trend line, but a 50% threshold is implicitly far below what “expert” means in any human-professional context. Acemoglu’s reframe is sharper: real expertise requires superhuman reliability. Evaluation should report reliability curves across task lengths rather than single-number horizons.

  • The bubble case, more precisely. “They don’t really have a monetization model” overstates the issue: ChatGPT alone is in the billions of dollars in ARR by mid-2026, plus OpenAI/Anthropic enterprise/API revenue. The case for an AI bubble runs on the gap between industry capex (hundreds of billions of dollars over 2024–2026) and current revenue (low tens of billions) at scale, plus the question of whether each query is profitable enough on a marginal basis to recoup compute cost. Acemoglu’s macro-avalanche scenario sits closer to Citrini’s bearish 2028 downside than to Citadel’s rebuttal, but with a different mechanism. Citrini’s trigger is rapid AI replacement of white-collar workers; Acemoglu thinks the replacement story is overstated, and the bubble is over-investment chasing capability that isn’t materializing.

Transcript

What’s here is the YouTube auto-caption transcript of the video, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog itself is verbatim — no words added, cut, or reworded — but five layers of editorial structure have been added on top:

  • Chapter outline. Twelve editorial chapters (H3 headings, each linking to its timestamp on YouTube). The video has no official chapter markers, so the boundaries and titles are editorial. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar.
  • Inline hyperlinks. First mention of every salient acronym, concept, paper, product, person, or company links to the most authoritative source.
  • Bracketed acronym expansions. Where an acronym appears for the first time without being expanded in speech, the expansion is inserted in [square brackets] (e.g. UBI [universal basic income]) to mark the addition as editorial.
  • Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag claims that are verifiable and slightly off, heuristics presented as fact, or attributions worth a reader’s spot-check.
  • Numbered references. Acemoglu’s main academic work cited here has a [[N]](#ref-N) cite linking to the References block at the bottom.

Acemoglu carries effectively all of the dialog. The host — Dave Briggs, former CNN/NBC/Fox News anchor and AIU Community founder — surfaces only once in the auto-caption track (“Do you see that happening?” at 24:52, marked Host: below). Acemoglu’s “Well, thanks Dave” at 17:40 is him addressing Briggs, not a turn change. The thinness of the host’s presence is conspicuous given AIU’s other episode (Briggs interviewing Rebecca Winthrop, 1h 9m) is a true back-and-forth — so this 37-minute cut is plausibly a curated edit of a longer raw conversation, with most of Briggs’s prompts removed. I couldn’t find a longer source online to confirm.

Filler tokens (uh, um, mid-sentence stutters) and obvious ASR mishearings of proper nouns are cleaned silently: Jamie Diamond → Jamie Dimon, Sam Alban → Sam Altman, Dario Amade → Dario Amodei, Chach GPT → ChatGPT, claude → Claude, deepseek → DeepSeek, blue color → blue collar. Punctuation, capitalization, and paragraph breaks are editorial — auto-captions ship without them. The video is 37 minutes.

Selectively italicized passages within each chapter are editorial highlights — verbatim text, just visual emphasis on the most arresting phrases.

0:00 — Reactive vs. proactive AI philosophy

There are two ways in which you can think about the AI philosophy. One is reactive. The other one is proactive. The reactive is AI is going in certain ways. It’s going creating certain dangers and we have to put guard rails in front of it. We have to do some amount of that. But that’s never going to be good. Why not? Because this is the most important conversation we can have and it’s the critical conversation we should have. AI will reshape every aspect of our lives.

And what Jamie Dimon is outlining is definitely a possibility. There is a lot that AI can do and there will be much more that AI will be able to do. Not just the speed but the direction of AI right now is a threat to jobs, is a threat to livelihoods and ultimately is a threat to liberal democracy because our system of government cannot survive in a world in which there are massive massive inequalities and a lot of people don’t have anything useful to do.

So we really have to make sure that AI creates jobs as well as productivity gains and other improvements in our lives. We are beginning to see the tip of the iceberg in terms of what AI could bring to the labor market. Some of this is indeed the ability of new AI models to do coding very well and thus reducing some of the demand for software engineers. But I think there’s going to be a lot of demand for software engineers because also AI is advancing so rapidly and integrating it into what organizations do, integrating into what people do in their lives — that’s a difficult thing and you need software engineering for that. But also the tech sector had hired a lot and they are restructuring in various different ways. I would suggest caution in interpreting all of the layoffs as being due to AI.

But the future is exactly what you’re outlining, which is that if AI moves towards what many technologists hope that it will do — AGI [artificial general intelligence] or later ASI [artificial superintelligence] — and starts doing everything that humans can do much better than humans, well, what use is there for humans? That’s a very scary world in some sense. Sure, it can bring some sort of abundance, and again we’re not seeing that right now. We’re not seeing huge productivity gains so far. We’re seeing more of the negatives than the positives.

But I think there is a different way in which we can use AI which would not be as disruptive to jobs and it would not be so disruptive to our lives. It would be human complementary, meaning that it actually works with us rather than tries to replace us. There are two choices here that would really determine what happens to entry-level positions. One is in what direction we develop these models. That’s very much a choice. There is nothing predetermined or inevitable about the way that AI is developing. And second is the choice that CEOs as well as other executives will make about how they’re going to restructure their companies.

My most likely scenario would be that AI’s spread in the economy is going to be slow because every complex technology requires a lot of organizational adjustment. A lot of things that companies used to do the way that they used to do them — they don’t want to change and they’re not going to have an easy time changing. And the AI models themselves have still a lot of limitations. So that means a slow path towards more and more AI in our lives. That doesn’t mean there’s nothing to worry about. Slowness gives you time to make the right adjustments in our society and also in the direction of AI. But right now, we’re not doing any of that. There has been no intelligent, interesting, forward-looking AI regulation under any of the administrations in the United States. So I’m not sure how we’re going to use the additional time that we have if things actually turn out to be slow.

Note

Editor’s note. “What Jamie Dimon is outlining” refers to Jamie Dimon’s public warnings throughout 2025 and 2026 that AI will reshape labor markets and that financial-system risk is poorly priced — the host frames the conversation as a response to those remarks. The host’s exact framing wasn’t captured in this segment of the auto-transcript.

3:09 — AI in schools: what the early evidence shows

I think before answering how we should prepare, we should look at what’s going on with our education system. The evidence is starting to come in that AI’s spread in middle schools and high schools and probably also in colleges has not been good for the students. There is a new study from China which is pretty large scale which shows that when students use AI for their homework, they start doing well in the homework exercises — they save time — and then their scores in exams and in all the general knowledge assessments tank. There are studies from smaller samples in the United States that show that neural activity changes in kids’ brains when they start using AI, and not in a good way.

So first of all we have to actually make sure that our schools function in the age of AI, and that requires also again to ask the same questions: what is it that we want to do with AI, and what is AI capable of doing for us? We’re not having that conversation.

Secondly, absolutely I think we have to be prepared for a job market that’s going to be reshaped by AI. And what that means is we have to think about what are the skills that AI is going to make redundant and what are the skills that AI is going to increase the demand for. Social skills, communication, working in teams — those are things that AI cannot replace because we want the human contact. And I think also a lot of creativity-related things AI is not going to be able to do anytime soon. So we have to instill values of understanding how to work with AI in a flexible manner so that humans can use AI and exercise their creativity, their innovative capacity. Parents have a lot of responsibility here, because the evidence also shows that if you use AI in more limited ways, it’s not bad for kids.

The learning process for kids is about developing mental muscles, putting effort, learning how to learn, putting the effort in order to think about how it is that you can fail in solving a problem and then how it is that you can actually gain some understanding in which ways you can tackle it. So if you go to AI too soon, all of that effort part is missed and that’s when you get the bad outcome. So we have to develop new norms. Kids should understand that it’s for their own good that they shouldn’t just get AI to do all of their homework. But there is no possibility that schools can regulate and say no, you shouldn’t use AI, because everybody has access to AI on their phone. So how are you going to stop them using AI when they go home? So that’s where parents come in. That’s where new norms come in.

And then if we had a more functional way in which the AI models were rolled out, we could have put guard rails in them — for example, we could have made sure that children or youths below a certain age would need parental supervision to reach certain aspects of AI, etc. But it’s not the case, and I don’t think that genie is going to be easy to put back into the bottle.

Note

Editor’s note. Acemoglu doesn’t name the “large-scale China study” or the “smaller US studies” he cites. The description of the China study (homework scores rise, exam and general-knowledge scores tank when students use AI on assignments) is consistent with a growing 2024–2025 literature of randomized AI-in-classroom field experiments — e.g. Bastani et al., Generative AI Can Harm Learning (Wharton, 2024, Turkish high school); the China study Acemoglu cites would be a contemporaneous companion. The “neural-activity-changes” study likely refers to Kosmyna et al., Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt (MIT Media Lab, June 2025), which used EEG on 54 college-age participants — not children — and found weaker neural connectivity during LLM-assisted essay writing. Worth flagging that the participants were college-age, since Acemoglu generalizes the “kids’ brains” framing across both groups.

7:17 — Augment workers, don’t replace them

There are two ways in which you can think about the AI philosophy. One is reactive, the other one is proactive. The reactive is AI is going in certain ways. It’s creating certain dangers and we have to put guard rails in front of it. We have to do some amount of that, but that’s never going to be good. Why not? Because first of all, you’re not anticipating what it is that is going to come and what it is that we can do. It’s always going to be defensive and it’s always going to have a bias towards slowing down AI — which, you know, if it’s going to do damage to us, sure we should slow it down, but there are dimensions of AI that are going to be very beneficial, so we don’t want to slow that down.

So I think we need a more proactive philosophy, which means we have to start by asking what is it that we want from AI and what is it capable of. And I think the answer there is AI is capable of many many things. It is capable of displacing workers — we’re seeing that, and we’re going to see more of it. But it’s also capable of complementing workers, giving them more tools to be better at what they do.

Imagine, for example, that all electricians, even including novice electricians and trainees, have AI tools in their hands that can help them deal with much more complex problems that are increasing rapidly because we have so many new equipments. We have — we’re going to have — the electricity grid change. We have all of the cloud computing and AI-related electrical equipment. And they can deal with that in a much more effective manner. That’s a very different vision than saying we’re going to eliminate teachers, we’re going to eliminate healthcare workers, we’re going to eliminate white-collar workers. We’re going to actually try to make them better so that they can do new things. They can do what they do more effectively.

And that’s actually great because — look, I don’t know anybody who says, “Oh, there are too many electricians around.” No, everybody has a shortage. If something goes wrong in your apartment or house, you’re going to have a hard time finding an electrician because we need better electrical services. Same thing for plumbing, for certain blue-collar skills, definitely nurses and healthcare. So if we can augment these people in the right way, that’s going to be a very different vision. And actually here’s the good news: it’s much easier to do than developing the most complex large language models that can understand every nuance of speech and try to outperform lawyers in the bar exam, etc.

So actually turning AI into a tool for humanity is not that hard. We are trying to push AI in one specific direction and there are limitations to that direction. The reason why AI is making workers’ lives more complicated is because we’re trying to say AI should do their job, and AI is not capable of doing their job. So the workers first lose some of the tasks that they were performing before, and secondly they have to babysit AI in an organization that’s actually in flux. As a result the stress level goes up, they waste a lot of time trying to babysit AI, and they don’t get the productivity benefits.

The evidence is also that organizations — with some exceptions, and the exceptions are important and we should look into them — when companies adopt AI in the wild, in their actual business, not like experimenting with the models in the lab — when they do it in the wild, they’re not getting huge productivity benefits, because we’re trying to force AI to do things that it’s not currently capable of doing. And we’re trying to shift the burden to workers, some of which are actually losing their wages and they’re losing their good jobs.

10:50 — Inequality and which jobs are next

Look, previous waves of technology — especially related to digital tools, robotics — took a big toll on blue-collar workers and office workers that used to perform simple tasks. The United States experienced a massive increase in inequality. Now people are very concerned about white-collar, some managerial jobs partly because the managerial class has a louder voice in the United States. I think the threat to software engineers is real, but exactly like you say, call-center workers — who are very low pay — are similarly on the line.

And we’re living through exactly the same things. Every company is installing an AI-based customer service system and many of them don’t work very well. I don’t know anybody who says, “Oh great, I called United Airlines and I had an AI assistant — that was great.” No, everybody is just like dreaded. How can I talk to an actual person who can help me with my complex problem? So again, we’re doing the same thing. We’re rushing without being ready for the technology.

And here is the problem. Blue-collar work really requires this interaction with the physical world that is currently much harder because robotics is a very difficult field and integrating AI and robotics is quite challenging. But if in the next 5, 7, 9 years we have advances in robotics technology and this integration, blue-collar work is going to be very much in the crosshairs of AI as well, and that could be an even more massive disruption.

I think some of it may be cultural but some of it is also related to exactly what we are hearing from tech leaders, that it’s going to go after entry-level jobs. So those are the jobs that Gen Z should be getting. So if you shut off their ability to get into the labor market and advance their careers, of course they’re going to be very opposed to it.

Also, if you look at the US statistics, people are much more concerned about AI than internationally. And part of that is because indeed in the United States, we have really no guard rails against AI. And that makes people more anxious. So having a good policy framework would encourage people to engage with AI the right way. So I think we are missing many opportunities here.

13:26 — China, zero-sum thinking, and global AI governance

Well, look, let me first preface that by saying I have been very, very critical of the Chinese regime for over 20 years. I have no sympathy for the way that they suppress freedom of speech and many basic human and civil rights, and I think there are many things wrong in China. However, I also think that the current zero-sum framing of the relationship between US and China is quite pernicious.

Indeed, if you are completely convinced — and you are right — that we are at the cusp of artificial general intelligence and subsequently artificial superintelligence, there could be a case, there would be a case, for complete zero-sum thinking with China. Meaning that there is no way that we can win unless China loses. We have to do our best not just to advance ourselves but also be ahead of China and perhaps even sabotage their advancements.

But I think the world isn’t like that. I don’t think we are at the cusp of AGI, and I don’t think that whoever advances in AI is going to dominate the world in the next 10 years. In fact, if you look at China, there are many things in which they are ahead of us and there are many many things in which the United States is ahead of China. For example, we have much better large language models such as Claude or ChatGPT. Their DeepSeek etc. is partly based on what has happened in the United States. But on the other hand, if you look at how AI is being integrated into consumers’ lives even more, how AI is being integrated into factories — China is ahead of us.

So there’s a lot for China to learn from the United States and the US to learn from China. More importantly, if you’re worried about some of the things that Jamie Dimon was saying, some of the things that we are talking about, you need global AI governance. You cannot do that just with one country. So you do need US and China to talk to each other, and you need Europe and developing countries to be part of this because billions of people in those parts of the world will also be impacted by AI. So we really need a global outlook. That doesn’t mean a world government or anything like that — I wouldn’t be in favor of that. But we need cooperation internationally and we really need to move away from this zero-sum thinking, because even though the Chinese system has many horrible features, we have to live with China. There’s only one world. Would be debilitating.

Note

Editor’s note. “We have much better large language models” was true at the time of recording for the frontier of capabilities, though by mid-2026 the gap has narrowed considerably — DeepSeek’s R-series and Qwen 3.x have closed the reasoning gap on standard benchmarks while remaining open-weights, and the US “much better” framing is now more accurate for closed-source frontier than for open-source. Worth a reader’s spot-check against current benchmarks.

16:37 — Advice to college kids and the case for democratic conversation

I’m kept awake at night sometimes thinking about what AI will mean for our society, for our democracy, for inequality, for jobs. But I think fear is not a positive attitude because it sort of debilitates you. I think what we have to do is twofold.

First of all, it is imperative that kids — with the support of schools, teachers, and parents — learn how to use AI correctly, how to use it in a way that complements them, not makes them less expert, less capable of learning how to learn. And also start thinking about how it is that they can have a flourishing career if AI advances and does a lot of things but not everything. So in other words, we cannot dismiss the possibility that there will be artificial general intelligence, like Dario Amodei and Sam Altman are telling us. But if that’s not a certainty — and I think it’s much, much less than a certainty — we have to plan for a world in which AI does a lot of things and we as humans do a lot of useful things as well. So they have to start planning for that world.

What it is that we can do in that world, and a lot of things that involve creativity, innovation, judgment, social interaction, teamwork, interacting with other humans, learning from other humans — all of these things are still going to be very valuable, and they’re going to be even more valuable if you can use AI the right way to complement whatever you’re doing in these domains. So that’s I think what the positive agenda for these college kids must be.

There’s a second leg to this. If I am right — which I may not be, but if I’m right — that AI is a powerful and rapid technology and it’s going in the wrong direction, the only way we can fix that is via democratic conversation. What that means is that we as a society have to be informed about what it is that AI is capable of, when, how we can use it for our betterment, and we need to be involved in that decision — not as protest masses but as positive democratic process — that changes the values, encourages AI researchers and AI entrepreneurs to do the more humanly beneficial things. And for that, college kids, high school kids, all of us need to be better informed. We need to be part of a democratic debate about what AI will do, what AI can do, and what AI should do.

Well, thanks Dave, but first of all, thanks for doing this. Indeed, I think this is what you’re doing is so critical. For decades, US media was extremely permissive of whatever tech barons were doing — gave them carte blanche to reshape society, reshape industries. And then now all the talk in the media is about AI doom and existential risk. Neither of these two extremes are useful. We need to be somewhere in the middle. AI can do useful things for us, but we need to take control of it. And that’s why conversations like this are critical.

19:14 — Defining AGI and why it’s hard to reach

Now, about AGI, here’s the problem. I actually cannot give you a widely accepted definition of AGI. There are so many definitions of it around. But I think what it means in essence is that AI models reach capabilities that are at the very, very, very expert level in everything that humans do. Now does that everything include all cognitive things, or does it also include interacting with the physical world? That’s one question. And another: what does it mean to be at this very expert level?

Like for example, some organizations that track AI progress look at: well, how long does it take for AI models to do things with 50% reliability? Well, 50% reliability is not good. If you really are claiming to be expert, you need to have better, superhuman reliability in what you do. And you need to do physics at the level of Einstein. You need to do journalism at the level of the very, very, very best journalists, etc. So that’s the bar. And if indeed we reach that bar, then the question is going to be why do you need the humans?

But what I’m saying is — no, it’s going to be very difficult to reach that bar because AI models don’t have the same multifaceted learning capabilities that humans have biologically, and those are quite important for creativity and judgment. So they’re going to be able to do a lot of things, but creativity and judgment, innovativeness, and as a result a lot of the social interactions that we are engaged with in problem solving and interacting with others — those are going to still remain human expertise areas. And as a result, there are a lot of capabilities for AI to help humans.

But that may be wrong. It may well turn out that Sam Altman and Dario Amodei are right and AI models are going to be as creative as the most creative lawyer or most creative journalist or writer. Well, in that case, we’re toast.

Note

Editor’s note. “How long does it take for AI models to do things with 50% reliability” is a direct reference to METR’s time-horizon benchmark — measuring task length at which a frontier model maintains 50% completion rate. Acemoglu’s point lands: 50% is not “expert,” it’s coin-flip.

21:17 — How prosperous societies were built

Let me take a step back and say, how have we created in the past peaceful, prosperous societies with limited inequality? And the answer is we’ve never done that by just redistributing income. We’ve done that through the labor market. Periods in which American society, other economies generated rapid growth and high living standards for the middle class, lower middle class — they were times when industries were creating jobs and paying high wages. In the United States, for example, from 1945 to the late 1970s, blue-collar worker wages grew faster than managerial wages. So those were the times where the economy was really like a tide lifting all boats.

Of course redistribution is important. There will be people who are disadvantaged. There will be people who need health care. Those are very important. But at least until now, human society has no experience with creating massive riches concentrated in the hands of a few companies and a few people and then redistributing that and creating a healthy society.

Now, if we have to go that way, if that’s the only future, of course we have to think about universal basic income [UBI] or universal basic dividend. There are things that we can try and there are things we must try. But my hope still is that we can find a path for AI that will not just create riches for a handful of people but also possibilities for people to have good jobs. But we must start planning for the alternatives.

And there are reasons for taxing some of the profits or some of the other things that are engaged in the AI economy. One of the reasons is, for example, if you look at the US tax code, it treats labor much more unfavorably than capital. So if you are a company and you’re putting millions of dollars into compute and buying equipment that can replace your workers, you get subsidies from the government. You amortize those spendings. You get subsidies for the interest rate you pay on the loans that you get in order to finance that spending. There are no capital gains taxes. Whereas if you hire a worker, you have to pay payroll taxes. You have to pay for their health care benefits. And then the workers themselves have to pay income taxes. So that creates a big asymmetry. And what that asymmetry does is that it encourages companies to actually automate and invest much more in automation, much more in compute and related things, in order to replace workers, than hire workers or train workers.

So those are things that we can try to deal with, and one of the ways we can do for example is by taxing some of the profits or taxing the compute spending of the largest companies. So there are many strategies that we can try, but I want to emphasize the bottom line again. I think it would be a much healthier way to grow for the US economy if that growth itself was shared — meaning that we also created good jobs, high-wage jobs, employment opportunities, career opportunities for young people.

Host: Do you see that happening?

Not on our current path. Not on our current path. And that’s why it’s so important to have this conversation, to have this democratic conversation. Because while I don’t see that happening left to its own devices — because AI is controlled by a handful of companies and they’re all determined to go down the automation path, try to seek the holy grail of artificial general intelligence — I am also outlining, and there is a lot of evidence suggesting, that an alternative in which AI could complement humans, could help us create jobs, is possible. But we are leaving those socially beneficial possibilities aside because we’re not focusing on them. The United States has a rich history and there are many periods in which US society has come together and done things that people thought were not possible. And I think we are at a point that is very dangerous but also full of opportunities.

Look, liberal democracy is in crisis. AI is going to reshape every aspect of our lives and we don’t understand in what way, and we are really afraid of all of these things that could happen. So if we start changing — I think a coalition around it can form. Before 2024 I was fortunate enough to testify several times in the Senate, and in the Senate at least I didn’t see this complete resistance to thinking about new ways of dealing with social media, dealing with AI, from both parties. There were many people who were concerned about the direction in which we were going and were trying to produce ideas and could come around different proposals. But of course the level of polarization has increased one notch, and that’s not productive. And the current administration’s AI policy is more acceleration, more acceleration, and that’s not going to help either. But we have time. We don’t have a massive amount of time, but not everything’s going to be done tomorrow. So we can start this conversation, and perhaps in a year or two there will be a coalition to think about these things in a more proactive way.

Note

Editor’s note. The “1945–late-1970s, blue-collar wages grew faster than managerial” framing is consistent with the standard labor-economics account of the post-war “Great Compression”; specific numbers from the Goldin & Katz tradition show roughly equal wage growth at the median and bottom from 1945 to ~1973, with sharp divergence from the late 1970s onward. Acemoglu’s tax-code asymmetry argument is developed in his and Pascual Restrepo’s task-model series and his recent NBER work on AI [1].

26:30 — The AI bubble and its monetization gap

That there is or could be an AI bubble does not conflict with the proposition that AI has great capabilities. There is in part an AI bubble because we’re trying to push AI very rapidly in a direction that’s not necessarily its natural direction. What I’ve been arguing is that artificial intelligence, despite the word intelligence, is very different than human intelligence. If two things are different, you try to use them together. Phil Jackson would have gone in the annals of basketball as the worst coach in history if he said, “Oh, I have Scottie Pippen and Michael Jordan and Michael Jordan is better. I should get Michael Jordan to do everything.” No, you get them to work together for a better team.

So that’s what we need to do with AI and human skills. But what is the industry trying to do? The industry is trying to say, “No, no, we’re going to try to get AI to replace humans.” And for that we need to put more and more and more investment. And the amount of investment of course requires some degree of hype. And the more hype you have, the more investment you have. And the amount of investment is so high that they would need to make massive profits, as you pointed out, in order to amortize, in order to recoup that.

But $1 trillion of profits or half a trillion dollars of profits is so far from what we are seeing currently — and they don’t really have a monetization model. People are not going to pay huge amounts in order to be able to ask ChatGPT which restaurant to go to. So how are they going to make this money? So there is a problem there. And if that bubble bursts, that’s really a double whammy because our economy is so dependent on AI a lot of people will lose their jobs, there will be a recession, and that would actually throw us back in many many different ways. And it would actually be even a bigger threat to our democratic institutions because hardship brings the worst in people, and there will be more polarization, more discontent. So it’s very important that we manage the AI enthusiasm the right way.

29:07 — Macro fragility and the 1970s parallel

For the reasons that you are also hinting at here, because people are concerned about their future and they’re also not making that much money. If you look at the US economy in the 1970s, there were all these middle-class jobs that not only paid decent wages but also promised career advancement and possibilities for their children. As a result, in the 1970s, in the 1960s, if you asked Americans, they would say in great majority of them would say our children are going to be better off than us. They’re going to have better jobs, better health care, better social conditions. Today, close to two-thirds of Americans are saying, “No, our children are going to be worse off than us.”

And why? What are they basing that on? Because if you’re a blue-collar worker, you’re not making that much money. And many blue-collar workers have lost their jobs. Many office workers are afraid of losing their jobs. And even if they keep their jobs, their wages are not keeping up with productivity. Their wages are hardly keeping up with inflation. So that creates economic malaise.

This is one of the puzzles of economics, which is that we are getting less and less dependent on oil as an economy say compared to the 1970s. But oil prices still matter a great deal. They affect costs of food and other inputs. And when oil prices spike, that has a really bad impact on the economy. So this, of course, is a period of high oil prices, and it doesn’t seem like the Iran conflict is going to have an end anytime soon. So I’m really worried about the macroeconomic effects of this.

And there is a macroeconomic avalanche possibility. People become less optimistic. They spend less. As a result, that actually then spills over to the AI economy. People become less willing to take risks with their AI investments and that pulls back the hype that we were talking about. So all of this could avalanche and there could be real negative consequences from that.

Note

Editor’s note. “Two-thirds of Americans say their children will be worse off” is consistent with Pew Research Center polling over 2023–2026 — the figure has hovered between 60% and 72% across multiple administrations and survey instruments, so the round-up to “close to two-thirds” is faithful. The 1970s comparison is the canonical “American Dream” framing from Raj Chetty et al. showing absolute mobility (% of children earning more than their parents) fell from ~92% for the 1940 birth cohort to ~50% for the 1980s cohort.

31:14 — Liberal democracy in crisis

Well, I mean — AI is the most important topic for the future, but only by a smidgen. The other really big thing is that we are in the midst of a liberal democratic crisis. Liberal democracy in my mind, without any doubt in my mind, is the best system that we could live under. Every other alternative is going to restrict freedoms. It’s going to favor some group versus another. It’s going to have less ability for us to generate new ideas, new innovations, and disseminate them throughout communities. And we’ve done quite well with liberal democracy throughout the 20th century.

If you go back to the 1990s or 1980s, everybody around the world was saying, “Well, we want the liberal democratic institutions.” They were looking at the United States. They were looking at some Western countries and saying, “We want those institutions.” And that’s why they went into the streets and protested against the army or the generals that were trying to run their country, or they rose up against the Soviet repression. But now a lot more people are saying, “Well, we don’t know about liberal democracy” or “We’re not that keen on it. Perhaps we need an authoritarian leader.”

Why is that? Well, because I think liberal democracy is in crisis. Part of the crisis is that we have underperformed as a liberal democratic society in the United States, in Europe, in many other parts of the world in generating shared prosperity. The kind of things that I was talking about in the ’50s, ’60s, ’70s where wages and job opportunities rose for people — that came to an end in the 1980s and 1990s, partly because of new technologies, partly because of trade, partly because of other things.

We’ve also done badly in terms of providing public goods, infrastructure, housing, healthcare, education. And people feel — especially in the United States — they don’t have voice. They used to actively participate in local politics, make decisions about how to live their lives in their communities, in their neighborhoods, and they had a sense that politicians were listening to them. And all of that has gone away. Some of it truly because politics became more segregated, more less responsive, and some of it because of social media and more discontent being fueled. But whatever it is, people feel liberal democratic institutions are not working.

And I think the hope that we can have for the future — and you can point out the same thing as you did for AI, that this is a little bit too optimistic given how dysfunctional we are as a society right now, how polarized we are, how badly Congress is doing — but again, the only hope that we can have is to remake liberal democracy in a better way. And that means again have liberal democratic institutions that are more inclusive. They are not segregated by Republican versus Democrat, or educated versus uneducated, managerial versus blue collar, religious versus non-religious. So we need to bring people together within communities and within the nation, and we need to make sure that that is undergirded by good jobs and better employment opportunities. So we’re back to the same things that I was talking about, and that’s why liberal democracy’s future and AI’s future are so tightly interwoven. If AI goes in the direction of destroying jobs and creating more inequality, I am afraid liberal democracy has no hope either.

34:24 — Closing: change the conversation

Well, I think policy and technology follow our society’s values. If we have the right values, and if we have the right information, the right aspirations, and the right way to communicate between us, I think everything becomes much easier. So I have every belief, every hope that if tomorrow we woke up and a very considerable talent in the tech sector said we understand certain directions of AI are not going to be good for humanity and there are better things for us to do, and we can work with society to make AI more human-friendly — we would get there. There is so much talent that if people put their focus on that, we will get there.

And I also believe that if society comes around the right conversation, many of the people in Silicon Valley are actually well-meaning. They would be encouraged to do the right thing. Not everybody, but many of them. So it’s really about starting to change the conversation. That’s why it’s so important to break this cycle of the media going from amazing tech enthusiasm of everything’s going to be better because of these tech geniuses to doom and gloom. No, we need to be in that middle space where we understand the capabilities of the technology, but we need to do our part of developing the right responsibility, the right values, the right governing philosophy for our future, including the future of AI.

I would encourage everybody, from middle schoolers to all the way the demographic curve, to use AI in a way that actually expands your understanding, your knowledge, your capabilities. Don’t let AI do the things for you. Do use AI so that you become a better decision maker, a better problem solver. Don’t get AI to decide your life. Get better information from AI so that you can make the right decisions, solve the problems, and ultimately in the job market have greater capabilities to put those skills, those understandings, those greater expertise [into work].

References

Talk and source

  • YouTube video (37m; AIU Community, May 6, 2026)
  • Channel: AIU Community on YouTube

People

  • Daron Acemoglu — MIT Institute Professor; 2024 Nobel laureate in Economic Sciences; co-author of Why Nations Fail and Power and Progress
  • Dave Briggs — host; former CNN, NBC, and Fox News anchor; founder of the AIU Community channel
  • Jamie Dimon — JPMorgan Chase chairman and CEO; the framing voice the host references
  • Sam Altman — OpenAI CEO
  • Dario Amodei — Anthropic CEO

Concepts and background

  • Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
  • Artificial superintelligence (ASI)
  • Universal basic income (UBI)
  • METR time-horizon benchmark — the “50%-reliability time” measure Acemoglu alludes to
  • Pew Research Center, “Views of children’s financial future” (2025) — recurring polling on intergenerational economic optimism
  • Raj Chetty et al., “The Fading American Dream” — absolute mobility (% of children earning more than their parents) by birth cohort, Science 2017

Companies and products

  • OpenAI — ChatGPT
  • Anthropic — Claude
  • DeepSeek

Papers

  1. Acemoglu, D. “The Simple Macroeconomics of AI.” NBER Working Paper (NBER WP 32487), May 2024. https://www.nber.org/papers/w32487

Related Posts

  • What Remains Scarce After AGI: Alex Imas and Phil Trammell on Labor, Capital, and Redistribution: two economists on the same labor-share question, more optimistic than Acemoglu that the labor market need not collapse, and turning on demand elasticity rather than the tax code.
  • Will AI Take Your Job? It’s Not So Simple: Steve Miller making the same augment-versus-automate argument three years earlier, the framing Acemoglu builds his whole case on.
  • GPTs Are GPTs: Labor Market Impact of Large Language Models: the OpenAI exposure study that quantifies which occupations AI touches, the empirical backdrop to Acemoglu’s worry about which jobs go next.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: a detailed bubble-burst downside scenario whose macro-avalanche mechanics parallel Acemoglu’s, though Citrini’s trigger is rapid worker replacement and Acemoglu thinks that story is overstated.
  • Is AI Cannibalizing Human Intelligence?: a counterpart to Acemoglu’s schools-and-learning worry, arguing the same erosion of human capability from the clinical rather than the labor-market side.

item.title: Yann LeCun on What Comes After LLMs
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In the May 15, 2026 episode of Jacob Effron’s Unsupervised Learning podcast, Yann LeCun — Turing Award winner and former Chief AI Scientist at Meta — lays out the technical thesis behind his new company, AMI Labs, and his reasons for leaving Meta after twelve years of building FAIR. The 1h 21m conversation moves from his core claim that LLMs are not a path to human-level intelligence, through the JEPA [1] architecture he is scaling, his sovereign-AI project Tapestry, why he diverged from Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio starting in 2023, and a remarkably candid account of his actual role at Meta — which, contrary to the public narrative, included zero technical contribution to Llama.

Tip

New to JEPA? Read the companion explainer first: What Is JEPA? covers the architecture, the latent-prediction objective, the collapse problem, the three families of fixes, and what V-JEPA and V-JEPA 2 demonstrate.

The main points, each linking to the supporting passage in the transcript:

  • LLMs aren’t a path to human-level intelligence — they can’t predict the consequences of their actions, can’t plan by search, and only work where language is the substrate of reasoning (math, code, problem-solving with a verifier). Useful products; not a research path.
  • JEPA learns abstract representations rather than predicting pixels. Five years ago LeCun realized every successful image/video representation method was non-generative; that crystallized into the joint-embedding predictive architecture.
  • Most “world model” robotics work today is imitation learning at huge data cost. A 17-year-old learns to drive in 20 hours; we have millions of hours of driving data and still no level-five autonomy. The bottleneck is data efficiency, not scale.
  • Tapestry is a federated training platform for sovereign open-source AI: contributors keep their data local, exchange only parameter vectors, converge to a global consensus model that countries can then fine-tune for local language, culture, and politics.
  • OpenAI is the next Sun Microsystems — closed proprietary models will get commodified by open ones the way Linux ate Solaris and HP-UX. Internet infrastructure has a natural pull toward open, and AI is becoming infrastructure.
  • LLMs are intrinsically unsafe — not because of doomer scenarios, but because they cannot predict the consequences of their actions, cannot guarantee task completion, and there is always a prompt that gets them to do something stupid. Objective-driven AI with explicit world models can be safe by construction.
  • Yann had zero technical contribution to Llama, positive or negative. His one Llama-related action was arguing internally for open-sourcing Llama 2 against the legal and policy departments. The popular narrative that he “ran” Meta’s LLM work is wrong.
  • Don’t work on LLMs for your PhD — academia can’t compete on GPUs, and explaining why LLMs work is descriptive science. Work on the next generation. LeCun’s current bet: SIGReg [17] (Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization) and other information-maximization regularizers — descendants of Becker & Hinton’s 1992 mutual-information objective [13] — to prevent representation collapse in JEPA, with LeWorldModel [19] as the latest demonstration.

Editor’s note. The intuition behind the regularizer family: collapse is the limit case where the encoder outputs carry zero information about the input — every input maps to the same , so the entropy of the representation distribution is zero. If you can force the encoder’s output distribution to have high entropy — i.e., spread across the latent space rather than concentrated on a single point — collapse is mechanically excluded. The technical obstacle LeCun flags is that differential entropy of a continuous distribution isn’t easy to estimate from samples — you can only construct upper bounds (estimators that overstate true entropy).
